Industry by Industry

Deeper service starts with understanding the workday.

These are starting points, not fixed packages. Volume, storage, route fit, inventory ownership, and return preferences are reviewed with every account.

01 / Hospitality

Hotels & Boutique Stays

Guest-ready sheets, towels, robes, bath mats, and food-and-beverage linen for properties where presentation and turnaround meet every day.

Occupancy changes the volume. Housekeeping sets the handoff. Storage limits affect how clean goods can return. A useful hotel program accounts for all three while keeping guest-facing items consistently ready for the next room.

Goods in the program

  • Sheets
  • Pillowcases
  • Duvet covers
  • Bath towels
  • Bath mats
  • Robes
  • Blankets
  • Table linen

What shapes the account

  • Occupancy-driven volume and room turns
  • Housekeeping storage and cart flow
  • Wrinkle control and guest presentation
  • Inventory levels across linen categories

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Route rhythm

    Pickup and delivery can be planned from weekly to daily service based on volume, route fit, and property needs.

  2. Care & finish

    Goods are sorted by type and use, then cleaned and finished around the property’s presentation standard.

  3. Return ready

    Folded, bundled, cart-ready, or account-sorted so housekeeping can put clean inventory back into rooms efficiently.

Common service mixLinens & beddingTowelsUniforms

02 / Property Operations

Short-Term Rentals & Property Managers

Bulk laundry support for operators moving guest linens between turnovers, properties, and a central staging location.

The challenge is not only washing. It is having the right clean goods staged when cleaners need them, without sending staff to laundromats or asking every property to manage laundry on site.

Goods in the program

  • Sheets
  • Pillowcases
  • Towels
  • Bath mats
  • Duvet covers
  • Blankets

What shapes the account

  • Checkout and cleaner schedules
  • Seasonal turnover volume
  • Property or item-level organization
  • Clean and soiled staging capacity

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Central handoff

    Bulk pickup and return are coordinated through an operating hub or other central location—not house-to-house service.

  2. Turn-ready finish

    Guest linens are folded, pressed where requested, and bundled around the way the turnover team stocks each stay.

  3. Clear organization

    Return can be labeled by property, item type, or another agreed structure that helps the team stage inventory.

03 / Wellness

Spas, Massage & Wellness

Treatment linens, towels, robes, wraps, and other soft goods returned clean, consistent, and ready for the next appointment.

Appointments create a steady linen rhythm. The program has to support room turnover, clean presentation, and shelf organization while freeing practitioners and front-desk teams from washing and folding between clients.

Goods in the program

  • Bath towels
  • Treatment sheets
  • Face cradle covers
  • Robes
  • Blankets
  • Spa wraps

What shapes the account

  • Appointment and room-turn volume
  • Oil, product, and odor attention
  • Soft hand feel and clean presentation
  • Fold consistency and storage space

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Usage planning

    Route cadence and inventory needs are reviewed against appointments, treatment rooms, and available clean-goods storage.

  2. Item-aware care

    Towels, sheets, robes, and treatment goods are handled around their fabric, use, and typical soil profile.

  3. Shelf-ready return

    Folded, pressed where required, bundled, and sorted by item type so staff can restock without reworking the goods.

04 / Fitness

Gyms, Yoga & Fitness Studios

Dependable towel programs for facilities where class volume, member use, and limited back-of-house space keep clean inventory moving.

High-use towels can turn staff into a laundry team. A route program moves that work off site and plans clean replenishment around member traffic, class schedules, and the space available to hold inventory.

Goods in the program

  • Workout towels
  • Hand towels
  • Yoga towels
  • Locker-room towels
  • Cleaning cloths by review

What shapes the account

  • Classes, memberships, and peak-hour use
  • Odor and heavy-use soil attention
  • Fast, consistent folding
  • Storage and replenishment space

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Demand rhythm

    Weekly demand is estimated from class and member usage, then matched to a practical route and inventory plan.

  2. Towel-focused care

    Processing is built around high-use towel soil, odor attention, and a dependable clean return.

  3. Ready to stock

    Towels return folded and bundled in a format that works with the facility’s shelves, front desk, or locker-room handoff.

05 / Events

Event Companies, Venues & Convention Centers

Specialty cleaning and finishing for presentation linens moving through event deadlines, weekend volume, and exacting visual standards.

Event goods carry the marks of a single service and then have to return ready for the next production. Sorting, stain attention, color-aware care, pressing, and the return window all matter as much as the wash itself.

Goods in the program

  • Tablecloths
  • Napkins
  • Runners
  • Skirting
  • Chair covers
  • Specialty event goods

What shapes the account

  • Event dates and return windows
  • Post-event sorting and stain attention
  • Color consistency and pressing quality
  • Peak-weekend and seasonal volume

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Deadline first

    Pickup and return are discussed against production dates, event schedules, and the volume arriving after each use.

  2. Specialty review

    Goods are reviewed by fabric, color, condition, and soil; specialty treatment paths can be evaluated where needed.

  3. Presentation return

    Pressed, hung or folded, and sorted by item type so the customer’s team can prepare the next order or event.

06 / Food Service

Restaurants & Food Service

Recurring care for kitchen uniforms, aprons, napkins, bar towels, and dining-room linen that work hard through every service.

Back-of-house soil and front-of-house presentation live in the same account. The program should separate how garments, towels, napkins, and table goods are cared for while returning everything in a format the team can use before service.

Goods in the program

  • Chef coats
  • Aprons
  • Napkins
  • Bar towels
  • Tablecloths
  • Kitchen uniforms

What shapes the account

  • Food, grease, and heavy-use soil
  • Weekly service and kitchen volume
  • Dining-room presentation standards
  • Garment and flatwork finishing needs

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Service cadence

    Recurring pickup and delivery are matched to kitchen usage, dining volume, storage, and the restaurant’s operating week.

  2. Use-specific care

    Garments and flat goods are separated for the stain attention, wash, and finishing appropriate to how they are used.

  3. Shift-ready return

    Pressed, folded, bundled, or returned in agreed carts or bags for a clean handoff to kitchen and dining teams.

07 / Workwear

Uniform Accounts

Professional cleaning and finishing for teams that need branded garments, chef wear, workwear, and department uniforms returned clean and organized.

Uniforms represent the business while taking repeated wear. A strong program considers garment construction, soil type, staff usage, finishing, packaging, and the way departments receive clean garments.

Goods in the program

  • Uniform shirts
  • Chef coats
  • Aprons
  • Workwear
  • Jackets
  • Branded garments

What shapes the account

  • Staff count and weekly usage
  • Repeated wear and stain attention
  • Professional finishing standards
  • Department or location organization

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Wear pattern

    Staff count, change-outs, garment types, and weekly use help define route cadence and inventory needs.

  2. Garment care

    Cleaning and finishing are planned around material, soil, repeated wear, and the presentation expected on shift.

  3. Organized return

    Hung or folded and packaged according to the account’s department, location, or team handoff requirements.

Casinos & Entertainment

Large-volume laundry and uniform support for venues with steady guest traffic, multiple departments, and high presentation standards.

Casino and entertainment accounts can combine uniforms, food-and-beverage linen, towels, and specialty garments across several departments. The program has to keep those streams organized without losing the overall service rhythm.

Goods in the program

  • Casino uniforms
  • Food-and-beverage linen
  • Towels
  • House goods
  • Specialty garments

What shapes the account

  • Large recurring volume
  • Department separation and change-outs
  • Guest-facing quality standards
  • Account-specific packaging and return

How Shelton shapes the program

  1. Account mapping

    Departments, goods, volume, change-outs, and handoff points are reviewed before setting the program structure.

  2. Separated care

    Uniforms, flat goods, towels, and specialty pieces follow the cleaning and finishing path appropriate to each category.

  3. Department return

    Pressed or folded goods can return with department-specific handling and account-defined packaging.

09 / Trade Partner

Wholesale Dry Cleaners & Laundry Partners

Behind-the-scenes production support for cleaners that need dependable laundry, pressing, finishing, specialty, or overflow capacity.

Wholesale work is a partnership inside another cleaner’s customer promise. Production reliability, finishing consistency, organized return, and clear expectations matter because the end customer experiences the result under the partner’s name.

Goods in the program

  • Customer garments
  • Pressed shirts
  • Household goods
  • Specialty items
  • Overflow work

What shapes the account

  • Production and overflow volume
  • Finishing and packaging standards
  • Organized partner return
  • Schedule and capacity requirements

How Shelton shapes the partnership

  1. Scope the work

    Goods, services, volume, timing, and the partner’s customer-facing quality standard are defined together.

  2. Match production

    Laundry, pressing, finishing, or overflow support is organized around the capacity the partner needs.

  3. Protect the handoff

    Work returns pressed, folded, packaged, and organized according to the agreed wholesale workflow.

10 / Custom Commercial

Specialty Commercial Accounts

Flexible commercial care for theaters, religious organizations, clubs, and operations with unique fabrics, schedules, or presentation needs.

Some accounts do not fit a standard category. Costumes, choir robes, club linens, banquet goods, and specialty garments need a conversation about material, use, timing, finishing, and packaging before the service is defined.

Goods we can review

  • Costumes
  • Choir robes
  • Club linens
  • Banquet goods
  • Uniforms
  • Specialty garments

What shapes the account

  • Unique fabric or construction
  • Performance, service, or event schedules
  • Presentation and finishing needs
  • Seasonal or as-needed volume

How Shelton evaluates the program

  1. Review the goods

    Material, construction, color, condition, use, and current care approach are considered first.

  2. Define the standard

    Cleaning, finishing, presentation, packaging, and turnaround expectations are agreed before recurring service begins.

  3. Plan the rhythm

    Scheduled or as-needed pickup and return can be discussed around performances, services, events, and seasonal demand.
